passages.text: The 10 Largest Deserts In The World Deserts are usually considered to be hot, arid areas with vast stretches of sand and dry earth. While this is certainly the case for some regions, all do not fit this description. Precipitation, not sand and heat, determine what areas are deserts. Deserts are found in all continents of the world but the nature and size of these deserts vary greatly. Since deserts are associated with difficult living conditions, they are often some of the world's most sparsely populated regions. In this article, we explore the world's largest deserts. passages.text: The Sahara is the familiar answer to a question about vast, hot deserts. Add polar deserts, however, and Antarctica takes first place. The apparent contradiction comes from treating “desert” as a temperature or landscape label rather than a description of a very dry environment. Antarctica is the world’s largest desert, commonly described at a continental scale of about 5.4 million square miles (14 million square kilometers). The Sahara is the largest hot desert. Ice does not disqualify Antarctica: its interior receives very little precipitation. These broad geographic labels do not mean every coastal location has the same desert climate. [citation needed] Climate The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert.[17][18] It is located in the horse latitudes under the subtropical ridge, a significant belt of semi-permanent subtropical warm-core high pressure where the air from the upper troposphere usually descends, warming and drying the lower troposphere and preventing cloud formation. [citation needed] The permanent absence of clouds allows unhindered light and thermal radiation. The stability of the atmosphere above the desert prevents any convective overturning, thus making rainfall virtually non-existent. As a consequence, the weather tends to be sunny, dry and stable with a minimal chance of rainfall. Subsiding, diverging, dry air masses associated with subtropical high-pressure systems are extremely unfavorable for the development of convectional showers. The subtropical ridge is the predominant factor that explains the hot desert climate (Köppen climate classification BWh) of this vast region. It is common knowledge that the melting ice caps are shrinking the polar deserts, but global warming is also leading to higher rates of desertification—the process where fertile land becomes dry and arid. Pollution and other human activities are creating droughts and wildfires, and increasing levels of salt in the ground, which is ultimately causing subtropical and semiarid desert regions to expand and rise in temperature. [citation needed] The rainfall inhibition and the dissipation of cloud cover are most accentuated over the eastern section of the Sahara rather than the western. The prevailing air mass lying above the Sahara is the continental tropical (cT) air mass, which is hot and dry. Hot, dry air masses primarily form over the North-African desert from the heating of the vast continental land area, and it affects the whole desert during most of the year. Because of this extreme heating process, a thermal low is usually noticed near the surface, and is the strongest and the most developed during the summertime. The Sahara High represents the eastern continental extension of the Azores High,[citation needed] centered over the North Atlantic Ocean. How to compare desert sizes fairly Check the category, boundary and overlap A useful desert ranking needs more than a column of large numbers. Ask four questions before comparing the entries: - What is included? Polar deserts, hot deserts and sand seas are different categories. - Where is the boundary? A climatic boundary may include a transition zone rather than follow a coastline or political border. - Are entries independent? A named subregion can lie inside a larger desert. - Which source and method supplied the area? A rounded reference estimate is not a new satellite measurement. Rub al Khali illustrates the boundary problem well. Guinness uses about 216,000 square miles (560,000 square kilometers), while noting estimates as high as roughly 251,000 square miles (650,000 square kilometers). It explains that precise boundaries are difficult where the sand sea meets other desert areas. Quoting more digits does not resolve that difference. passages.text: Different processes can produce dry environments. Descending air in subtropical circulation tends to warm and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain extensive dry belts away from the equatorial rain zone. Mountains can also create a rain shadow: air rises, cools and loses moisture on one side, then descends drier on the other. Polar dryness has a different setting. Very cold air carries little water vapor, and the Antarctic interior is far from many moisture sources. These mechanisms can interact; a desert does not need to fit one simple cause everywhere within its boundary. Temperature categories also need care. The U.S. Geological Survey identifies the Great Basin as a cold desert, unlike the Mojave, Sonoran and Chihuahuan hot deserts. A place with hot summer days can still have cold winters and belong to a cold-desert category. The Great Basin should not be grouped with hot deserts merely because it lies in western North America.
